utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Sarah Clanton, Douglas Stringer, Case Manager Thomas Laugel, and legal intern Marina Marcikic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with Jolana Makraiova, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is your next witness ready, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Yes, indeed, she's ready. The witness has some difficulties standing --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I just ask for private session briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And the witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may be seated, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You may be seated, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Should I get closer or further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Witness. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. First of all, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Karmen Brlic-Jovanovic. 13th of July, 1948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic, you are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I have to point out to you that the solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalties of perjury, should you give misleading or untruthful information to this Tribunal. Please read the solemn declaration the court usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I stand? I don't have to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, you don't have to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you -- thank you very much. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we please have 1D1167 on the screen, which is Defence tab 3. And, Mr. President, I have a hard copy for the witness and for Your Honours, if I wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, do you recognise that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The witness statement which I gave last year to Madam Aleksandra Andric and it was certified by a public notary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are you familiar with its content?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you read it before you signed it in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does it accurately reflect what you said when you gave this statement?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you answer the questions that you were asked the same way again, if you were asked those same questions here today?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I tender, Mr. President, 1D1167 for admission, along with associated exhibits 1D455 and 1D456.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statement will become Exhibit D200. The associate exhibits will be given Exhibit Numbers D201.200, and D202.200. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you worked as a journalist at Radio Vukovar before the outbreak of hostilities --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And just so you know there interpreters around the room and a court reporter who is taking down everything that is said and they require that there be a pause between the end of my question and the beginning of your answer so that everything is recorded accurately. At the very last sentence of your statement, which is paragraph 4, you say: "The witness," so that's you, "remembers that love poems and interviews with Branko Kovacevic, a poet from Pacetin who was a doctor, were broadcast on Radio Vukovar and published in Vukovarske Novine." Can you tell us who conducted those interviews that you referred to here with Dr. Kovacevic on the radio?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you tell us how many times you interviewed Dr. Kovacevic on the radio, approximately?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Several times but not too many.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what was the content of those interviews? What was said by him; what was asked by you.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What he wrote about, how he felt about publication of his work as a young author that he was, whether he wanted to continue doing so as he was a medical rather than a literary expert, and he was full of verve and intended to keep on doing that forever because that was what he liked. Alongside his regular job as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Had his poetry been published in some form?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember one book from early on, and then, later on, I -- I didn't really follow it that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was any of his poetry recited during these interviews?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At literary evenings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But during the broadcasts themselves, leaving aside the literary evenings, was any of his poetry spoken, read, or recited?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as something that followed upon the information that I gave about those events. But he had to do it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have, please, 1D331, which is Defence tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, perhaps I could ask you: How well known was Dr. Kovacevic as a poet in eastern Croatia, let's say?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning, thanks precisely to me, because I wanted to encourage the young people and to present them to the public, such was also the case with Zoran Calic who is now a recognised man of letters, whose books are reviewed in many languages. He's recognised all over the world, and the reviews are written by renowned men of letters from various countries. My intention was always to assist someone who wanted to do something good. I wanted to help them to move on up as much as they could, and I believed that this was something that really deserved attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we zoom in just a little bit in this photograph on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's been reduced in size.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, looking at this photograph, do you recognise the gentleman in the white suit?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: To me it looks like Branko Kovacevic. And when this was taken and how fatter he got and how much he changed, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Mr. President, 1D331.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 4 of your statement, you say: "I had not known Goran Hadzic before I invited representatives of political parties to a confrontation in a radio programme which took place after Easter 1991 and the incidents at Plitvice." Did you interview Mr. Hadzic on that occasion that you referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Him as well as other prominent leaders of some political parties that were active in Vukovar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And leaving aside the others, can you tell us what political views Mr. Hadzic expressed to you on this occasion or expressed in general on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was in favour of compromise, agreement. He did not oppose anything that others would say. He was not too pushy, he did not impose his opinion on others in order to achieve anything that others would have to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he say anything about how to resolve the ethnic tensions that were rising during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Firstly to remove the weapons which instilled fear in people. Secondly, to place under control the individuals who acted inappropriately, inappropriately to a civilised environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic. I'd now like to move to a new subject, and I will not be asking you about the period during which Vukovar was under siege and you were there. I will not be asking you about that. But I would like to ask you about when it was that you came to leave Vukovar for the first time as the fighting subsided. Can you tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: While the combat operations lasted, my immediate family - that is to say, my husband, my son, my brother-in-law - together with more than 100 civilians, were evacuated to the first line of combat activities by the Belgrade Guards Brigade on the 12th of November, 1991. That was when we were taken in some vans to a collection point at Velepromet. That was around noon. We were given accommodation. I have to say it was sad and awful but that was the only possible thing at the time. We were given sacks of rice and pallets to sleep on. Outside fighting was still going on, and it was dangerous. That was before the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then how and when did you come to leave Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as we were concerned, the first time to leave was on the 14th, when lists were made of people who were leaving and where they would be leaving. Transportation in buses was organised, and the bus was driven by Djuro Filipovic. He was wearing a military uniform. He took care both of the list-making and he also confirmed that the persons from the list were, indeed, on the bus. He would do that at every check-point all the way to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: After you arrived in Sid, when was the first time after that that you returned to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of November. Because there was a report from the police station in Sid that the army had moved my mother-in-law and that the father had remained in Vukovar. During our stay in the big cellar - not in Velepromet but in the cellar, in the basement - at Pavle Radisavljevic's place, we were separated from my father-in-law and mother-in-law. They had stayed on in their ruin of a house because my father-in-law was practically about to die. He had wounds, an injury, he was bleeding, and he could not be helped at the time in any way whatsoever. My mother-in-law told him that he had died but that her request that he be buried could not be met because of the fighting that was ongoing. It was on the 15th that she told us that. And then she commanded us to go and fetch him on the 16th and either bury him or buy a coffin in Sid and then bring him over to Sid. That was the way she saw it. So in Sid, we went close to the fair-ground where there was an official office at which one had to ask for a pass allowing a person to leave Sid and go to Vukovar, as combat operations were still ongoing in that area. We got the pass. He -- they were asking who was going and we said that it was us, so we got the pass with our own names on it with the stamps and signatures of the officers who were on duty at the time. They all wore uniforms, the JNA uniforms. And military police was standing in the room. We then looked around to see who would take us to Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you there for one --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The traffic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- for one moment, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, and ask for a clarification. You say that --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- the military police were standing in the room. Was it the military police that signed or stamped the pass?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. There was a man sitting at the desk who was on duty and the military police were there to provide our security. Everything was under rather strict control. At least that's the way I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was the man sitting at the desk wearing a JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have 1D3735, please, which is Defence tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I rise to note that these materials are not on the Defence 65 ter list. They are part of the pending third motion for leave to amend filed by the Defence. Our response is due today so it has not yet been filed before Your Honours, but to note that we do object to the use of this document and, I believe, five other documents provided by the witness on the basis that they were not timely disclosed to the Prosecution. They were in the possession of the Defence for six weeks before we were provided with them, and it is not evident from the 65 ter summary or the 92 ter statement how they relate to her evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. President, there's no obligation to disclose documents as soon as they come into the hands of the Defence. There is no such obligation, so we didn't have an obligation to immediately disclose the documents. Now having said that, of course, we have an obligation to -- when we ask for an amendment of our 65 ter exhibit list, to ensure that we diligently and in a timely way provide those documents and that there is no prejudice to the Prosecution. Those are the two standards. And I can tell Your Honours that we requested that those documents be translated on the 4th of August, 2014, and we only did get a translation back on the 2nd of September. Now, it is true that that's too long, and somewhere during that time-period we realised that these documents had not been prioritised for translation and we asked that they be prioritised. And my understanding is that they were disclosed on or shortly after the date of the translation, namely, the 2nd of September. And then Your Honours will know that then the motion was filed, the 65 ter exhibit list motion, was then filed on the 5th of September, 2014, so that's about 17 days ago. And each of the four travel passes that I propose to use are less than a page long or one page -- a page, two sides but very little text. I would also say, Your Honours, that it was not certain that we would be moving to have these documents added to our 65 ter exhibit list through the month of August, and until we'd made certain decisions about calling this particular witness and about which documents to use. So that also was a reason for not having disclosed the document at the very -- at the beginning of August. And I do wish that we had been able to disclose it at the beginning of August but that didn't occur. In any event, there's been more than ample time now for the Prosecution to digest these documents. Now as to whether or not it's covered by the summary, the summary says that the witness will -- perhaps the witness should remove her headphones for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the question, of course, before -- before she removes her headphone or even without. Mrs. Brlic, do you understand English? Obviously not. Madam Brlic, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. A little. Very, very little. Things that pertain to new modern technology, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. May I then now ask you to remove your headphones. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The witness summary says that she will recall her experience taking refuge in a shelter for extended periods during the fighting around Vukovar in October and November 1991, her departure from Vukovar around 16 November 1991, and her return about eight days later. And then it continues and I won't go into what's described next. Now, as for the 65 ter exhibit list motion that was filed on the 5th of September, it says as follows at paragraph 8: "The witness supplied the Defence on 28 July 2014 with six original travel documents issued by the JNA in 1991 related to herself and her husband." And I must interrupt here, myself, to say that that's a mistake. It's only four travel documents that we're dealing with and two documents of another provenance. And then it says: "Those documents were promptly sent for translation and are sought for addition now that the translations for most of the documents have been received. The documents' authorisation issued by military authorities for the witness to reside in the conflict zone are demonstrative of the JNA's overarching authority over civilian movement and civilian matters." So there clearly there's notice of why we want to use these documents and how they relate to the witness's testimony. And then finally on Saturday night, unfortunately, it was between 8.00 and 9.00, there was further precision on the dates of the witness's travel which should have been indicated by reviewing the documents itself, albeit it does not correspond precisely to the dates mentioned in the witness summary. So taking all that, Your Honours, I suggest there's clear notice, no prejudice, ample time to prepare, and we should be permitted to add these documents to our 65 ter list and proceed now with questions in relation thereto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just to briefly respond to a few of counsel's points. As he indicated, by looking at the 65 ter summary, what it says is that she will discuss her departure and her return. It does not give any mention of the authorities, of an office in Sid, of the role of the JNA or the military police. And also to respond to the point about what was provided on Saturday evening between 8.00 and 9.00 p.m., what we have received is a handwritten document in B/C/S. There's no translation provided, and it refers to paragraph 4 of the proofing note which says that the witness wrote a chronology of her movements back and forth between Sid and Vukovar between the 12th and the 26th of November, 1991. It does not indicate what specifically is written in this B/C/S handwritten chronology. So the Prosecution is not able, between 9.00 p.m. on Saturday and 9.00 a.m. on Sunday, to have conducted any investigation or even to have had an adequate translation of the material that was provided by the Defence, and that is why we say that these materials should not be added as there is a prejudice to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, this is about five documents. Am I right? Five documents to be added to your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: There are six proposed. I would -- the ones that we've been talking about now encompass four. There's a fifth which involves different issues and the sixth I won't be using, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So about these four. Is the handwritten B/C/S document Ms. Clanton referred to, is that included in those four?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. And just to be clear about that, that document was produced by the witness on Saturday night in my presence, and I deemed it necessary and appropriate under the Rules to disclose any prior statement of the witness. So it was disclosed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And theres no intent to use it at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, what I understand from counsel's previous submissions, though, was that the materials that we're discussing, the four permits, that those can be understood in light of the information that the witness provided on Saturday in this note. And our point is that we cannot be expected to be on notice or to have had an opportunity to consider the four documents that are at issue in light of this information given that we aren't able to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. The four documents can be added to the 65 ter list. Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you kindly, Mr. President. May we then have 1D3735, which is Defence tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, the witness doesn't have her headphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, if you look at the screen in front of you, on the left side, is that the document that you have just described having received on the 16th of November in Sid?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you were about to continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you were, before I interrupted you, about to describe how you travelled back to Vukovar. How did you travel back to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no civilian transportation, and you couldn't go on foot either. If you had a pass and only then could you be transported in a military vehicle. That was the only option. And that vehicle would be stopped at every check-point all the way to Vukovar, and then had you to show your pass again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And leaving aside the details of what you did in Vukovar when you returned on the 16th, can you tell us when you left Vukovar next?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't manage to carry out the task that we had been given by my mother-in-law and that was either to bury or to find the body and bring it back. We did not have a reason to linger on. A jeep took us back, kindly, initially to take us to Sid. However, the curfew was in place and we were stopped in Negoslavci. That's where we spent the night with the Ore family, the family of Petar Ore. The following morning, we found transport in an APC or some such vehicle, and we returned to Sid. We stayed there, but before that, I have to add something that I failed to mention. When we arrived in Sid we were accommodated in Adasevci. We stayed with my husband's family. So when we returned to Sid, we spent several days in Adasevci. And then my mother-in-law insisted that we should go back again and, at all cost, try to find the body of her late husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when did you go back to Vukovar the next time, as best you can recall?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a lot of family pressure for a few days. And then, on the 24th, we decided to go back to Vukovar. We had to undergo the same procedure, i.e., we had to be provided with a pass, but on that occasion, it was just my husband and I who went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: And again the procedure was the same. The route we took was the same as the first time round. Again, we were taken to Velepromet because that was our only official address that we had at that time. You couldn't enter the city. We could not reach our houses at all because there were services that monitored the situation and looked after the safety of civilians. And they told us that our neighbourhood was not at all accessible. And then my husband insisted with the military to provide their own men who would --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I just, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, stop you there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And ask that 1D3728, please, which is Defence tab 8, be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, was that document on the left side of the screen the document that you received on the 24th in Sid to be able to return to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly that it was the 24th itself, in other words, the same day that you received the pass, when you travelled to Vukovar from Sid?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Everything had to be done right away because there was nowhere for us to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then on this journey which commenced on the 24th, how many days did you spend in Vukovar before you left again?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We asked for assistance. Actually, my husband asked for assistance from the military. However, when he left together with several soldiers, we were told that in cases like that, when a house was so badly burnt, no human remains are left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And -- and when was it after these activities, if at all, when was it that you left Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't be sure, but I believe that we returned ... and then we talked to my mother-in-law and tried yet again to do something on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there a subsequent occasion when you sought permission to travel back to Vukovar from Sid?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We had to. Every time. I went to the same office as a matter of course. The procedure was always the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have, please, 1D3729, Defence tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is a permit for temporary residence in the zone of combat operations, and the date is the 26th of November, 1991. The name listed is Radoslav Jovanovic. Who is that, Radoslav Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My husband. Now he is my late husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you remember having received this particular document?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D206, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have 1D3730, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is, again, a permit for temporary residence in the zone of combat operations dated 21 December 1991. Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, do you remember having received this document at around this time?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because we intended to decide where we would live, and we wanted to go back to Vukovar at any cost. So we went to learn how that is to be done, because we had no house any longer, we had no food, we had no clothes, but we wanted all that to be resolved in some way or another in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was this document issued in the same way and by the same people as you've described in respect of the previous documents?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was issued in the same way, but the location where it was issued was different. It was no longer the office near the fair-ground but an area in the park. It was a nice hunting lodge that I suppose belonged to the hunters and the hunters' association from the area. Everything else was still as strict as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the individuals who were at that office, were they the same individuals who had been involved in issuing the previous passes? Not necessarily the same people but the same description in terms of uniforms and so forth.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, travel back to Vukovar at around this time; namely, the date of this document, being the 21st of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And where did you stay on this occasion when you went back in December?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the relatives, at my husband's cousin who had returned a day or two before us. He had returned to his own house which was damaged, but one could use it to spend a night. There were mattresses on the windows which were no longer in place. We received some food from the Red Cross. We slept on the floor. It was cold and uncomfortable. Terrible, really. There was no water to be had at all, nor any electricity. So we kept close together in the same room. And, on the following day, we went around to look if there were any offices there where they would decide what they were going to do with us. One couldn't walk around the town. You had to hear from someone who is closest to you where he had gone, so you would go there too. So that was what we did. And everything was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you at some point seek to find, with your husband, some accommodation where you could stay yourself?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We, ourselves, actually didn't. We waited for others to solve that for us. The houses where the fighting hadn't been so bad or had stopped earlier had already all been full of people who had moved in. And for us who were late, there was nothing good where we could move in. So we waited for them to tell us: You can try here, or you can try there. And then we would see what we would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And where did you end up after this process of searching?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First we stayed at that cousin's place during all these days. Together with him and his wife, we would go to the Red Cross to get some clothes and the first rations. That was the food, flour, oil, soap for doing the washing, some canned food. When we left for Vukovar, we managed to persuade our relatives that if it was fine for us, that they should return as well. So then my brother-in-law went to find something for himself and his mother, and he got some sort of certificate saying that he could clean an area, because we wanted everything to be close rather than to be scattered all over, because the situation was really awful. He managed to get a house that was whole on the outside and, on the inside, it was only the lower ground floor that could be used 70 or 80 per cent. The windows had to be closed with rags and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I can just interrupt you, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic. Am I understanding that this is the house that you ended up living in, staying in?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was some form of authorisation required for you to be there? In that particular house.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was an authorisation about that particular house which was issued to my brother-in-law, to his name, and he had requested it. I have to note that during the days that followed, on several occasions military patrols had come unannounced. One could call them that because they were all uniformed. I was particularly unhappy about that because I was afraid. I didn't know and didn't understand why they would care about this, but they tried to calm me down, they told me not worry and that they said that those who were in town at the time were doing this, that we should not be afraid for our own security, that we could keep the door unlocked. And, actually, it was not even possible to lock them because there were no locks and very often there were no doors at all. In that building, even the toilet on the floor was half-ruined and there was no outer wall, but it was standing and it was some sort of roof over our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have, please, 1D3736, Defence tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us your brother-in-law's name?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Milovan Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this is a document which at the top left says: "Serbian District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem." It's entitled: "Certificate. This is certify that Milovan, son of Veljko, has been duly reported to this service and is properly recorded. We hereby request that the apartment at Preradoviceva 2 be cleared and cleaned without hindrance until the final decision of the commission." Do you remember this, your brother-in-law receiving this document or having this document?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And he was very proud of having managed to take care and having provided a place where we could all find accommodation and live. He, as the younger brother, had managed to provide for his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you yourself subsequently move out of Milovan's house and go somewhere else to stay?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This was the sort of accommodation that wasn't adequate even for two persons, let alone more than that. People of different ages, the elderly mother, myself, there was no room for beds or anything, and the roof leaked so that in bad weather I would spend all day on the steps trying to squeeze water out of various cloths because there was no roof. It was a two-storey house, and so I tried to keep it dry so that we could stay downstairs with a candle and we had a small stove which we used for heating.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, if I could just take you back, please, to my question, which was whether you at some stage moved out of Milovan's house and went to stay in a different house.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you can just tell us yes or no to that question --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you or your husband receive a document similar to this one in respect of the accommodation you moved into?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the same document. My husband and his brother went to obtain it. I didn't go, so I have no idea where the service that was in charge of resolving such issues may have been located.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you understand that this document, which is called a certificate, entitled you to live in that house permanently?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Not at all. It was clear to everyone that that was a temporary solution, regardless of even what some sort of commission may have decided. I believe that private property is inviolable. I still consider it such to this day and I don't think I will ever change my mind about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Mr. President, 1D3736.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which, Mr. Gosnell, is not one of the four -- is it one of the four?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You are absolutely correct, Mr. President. I apologise. I would seek leave to add this to the 65 ter list. It is one of the documents that is the object of our motion of the 5th of September, 2014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we don't object to the document being added at this time, in light of Your Honours' previous ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The document is admitted to the 65 ter list and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D208. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No further questions at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Are you ready, Ms. Clanton?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: My name is Sarah Clanton, and today I will be asking you some questions on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. If at any time my question is confusing or complex, please feel free to ask me to clarify. Now, the first thing that I want to ask you about today has to do with your background. I saw from your statement that you went to school in Vukovar and that you also lived in Vukovar at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And also that you were a journalist at Radio Vukovar since 1972; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the 2nd of June that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And it says in your statement that you were born in Osijek. Can you tell me when it was you moved to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before I was to be born, my father was sent to the Varazdin museum by a decree and I was supposed to be born there. However, my mother's relatives had a house and were living in Osijek so my mother went to her family to give birth there, and then she was to return to Varazdin. After Varazdin, when I was around one year old my father was transferred to Bjelovar to take charge of the museum there. After that, by a decision on the founding of the museum in Vukovar, at the initiative of Dr. Antun Bauer, Antun Bauer, my father was appointed as the director of the town museum in Vukovar in the 1950s. And so Mom and I also moved there. Since then, I have lived continually in Vukovar. And all my years of service, all my years of employment, were at Radio Vukovar and Vukovarske Novine. That is to say, the Vukovar newspaper, which had a single editorial office up until the events of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you referred earlier today to your late husband whose name was Radoslav Jovanovic. Where was your husband from, what town?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My husband was born in Vukovar. He never went anywhere. He had always lived in Vukovar. We attended high school together. We were classmates. Later on, he studied agriculture in Osijek, and his speciality was mechanization in agriculture. And he then got a job at Vupik.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, I believe you've said earlier that there was some sort of a family home that was in Sid. Was this a home of your husband's family or your family?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in Sid but in Adasevci, near Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That dealt with my objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And if I could clarify, ma'am, is this a home in Adasevci, near Sid, that was in your husband's family?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Adasevci. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Is it correct that this was a home related to your husband's family?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's perhaps 4 or 5 kilometres away from Sid. It's a huge village. And that was what my husband's mother - that is to say, my mother-in-law - inherited from her grandparents. She had married in Vukovar too, and her cousin -- her younger brother, actually, remained living at the family estate.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And was your husband of Serbian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And I see from the first page of your statement that you are of Croatian ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, during the time-period we're talking about here, which would be around the beginning of 1991 into the summer and the autumn of 1991 while you were in Vukovar, can you tell me if your husband belonged to any military group or any armed forces?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Because after recruitment, he had been relieved of having to serve the army for health reasons and he never had a single day of military obligation. He was permanently relieved of any obligations with the army after all possible medical examinations that had he to undergo in Zagreb several times. Eventually he confirmed, by his state of health and his life, the accuracy of the military medical examinations. He had two strokes and high blood sugar and high blood pressure and suffered from gangrene eventually and he was an invalid in a wheelchair. And he was an opponent of anything that could drag him away from his home, his family, his job at Vupik. He was in charge of the agricultural pharmacy. He had to undergo treatment several times at the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic. I'm sorry to interrupt you. I understand from your answer that because of health reasons, your husband had no military obligation, was not part of any military structure. I just want to be very clear: Did he support any volunteer group, or himself work as a volunteer during this time?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He didn't want to join any political parties. He never had anything to do with it. He never supported it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, we've heard during your direct examination -- my learned friend showed you a permit that was dated the 21st of December, 1991. And from that permit, am I correct in understanding that that is the time that you returned to Vukovar on a more or less permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, such was our family decision. However, we needed to find accommodation and then clean it all up and clear it up, and we really decided to be there and nowhere else. We reported ourselves for rations and for health services and for any possible job that might turn up in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Clanton. Madam Brlic-Jovanovic, this is the time for our first break. We take 30 minutes, and we will be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, before the break, I had asked you if it's correct that you and your family returned on approximately the 21st of December to Vukovar and stayed after that time, and you said that you took the decision as a family and you were then in Vukovar cleaning up your home, the home you were living in. I want to clarify that after that time, you were resident in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We went several times to fetch food from my uncle and we went to do our laundry where we could. In my uncle's house, we would do our laundry. We would receive some food. We tidied ourselves up and then we returned. It was already winter time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: There --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then we spent the Catholic Christmas holiday in Vukovar. I can tell you that I was pleasantly surprised that some of our acquaintances from before congratulated me. But just me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And when you say that you tidied yourself up "and then we returned," you mean returned to Vukovar where you were living?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement, it says that you qualified for retirement in 2008; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I turned 60, I still fell under those provisions of the law in Croatia. Currently it is different. You have to be older or have more pensionable years, but yes, I was retired right on time, when I -- at first opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the meantime - maybe you will be interested to know - in the meantime after 1991, I have not worked anywhere. My husband was very ill. Our living conditions were anything but good and then his health deteriorated, and then my brother-in-law went missing. We have still not been able to find him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, yes, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you did anticipate my question. If I understand your answer, you did not work as a journalist after 1991. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. On the 24th of August, 1991, was the last day I worked. And then on the 31st of August, 1991, was the day that was recorded in my work booklet as my last pensionable day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would like also to confirm at this time that you have no personal or social connection or relationship with Goran Hadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I saw him during those talks in 1991 - I believe that it was in April of that year - I've never seen him or met him again. I haven't had any reason to contact him after that. If people needed me, they could always find me. He didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what you've just mentioned, April 1991, that's the time-period that I want to talk about now. And you've testified about this, and it's also in your statement that you interviewed Mr. Hadzic after the incident at Plitvice. And my question for you is: Would you agree with me that at this time the environment was somewhat tense?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. However, the head count was still okay. And there was still a chance in the offing that people would agree and that nothing bad would happen. My desire then and still is, despite everything that I've been through, that we should all live normally, help each other, and respect each other. And in that sense, I invited representatives of all political parties. They were all accommodating, they all came, they all spoke in a civilised manner, and nobody insulted anybody else. I liked Goran Hadzic's stance. He was not as talkative as one would have expected. He was just a normal person, very civilised and well-mannered and soft-spoken.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now if could I have the assistance of the Registrar to pull up 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Are you okay, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I keep losing the sound. I'm trying to adjust my headphones. Now it's okay. I believe that I wouldn't have any problems hearing now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Okay. If you do have any difficulty, let us know and the usher can help you with the headphones.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then if something is amiss I adjust my headphones, but now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, during this time do you recall that ministers, including Croatian Minister of Interior Boljkovac and his deputy minister, Slavko Degoricija came to Vukovar to diffuse tensions that we've just discussed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present, not during the talks. I spent in the room adjacent to Mr. Boljkovac's room with all the other journalists. We all waited for the conclusions from the meeting. The journalists didn't have access to the talks themselves. And then the representatives of the Serbian villages or Serbian parties, or whatever, gave their own demands, to put it that way. And then I asked Mr. Boljkovac to allow --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could ask for the Registrar to bring up 1D02192. And this is at tab 12. I don't believe that's the correct document. 1D02192. Yes, that's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If we could have the assistance as well of the Registrar to zoom in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: -- I want to ask you a few questions about what you've just told us, this visit, and we see here a newspaper article. Can you tell me if you're able to see it, please.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have a magnifying-glass which I brought with me, but still I can't see anything. Maybe you could provide me with a hard copy. My eyesight is really not good. I can't see a thing. If possible, you could perhaps provide me with a hard copy and then I'd be able to answer by either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do have a hard copy available for the witness. If it would be possible for the usher -- and to note that I have written the 65 ter number on it but it's otherwise clean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, what I want to confirm is that what you were just telling us about the journalists who were waiting in the next room and that you were waiting to hear the outcome of the talks, that this article is about those same events?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On two occasions, and I was there on both those occasions, the first time there was a meeting with the military leadership of the JNA, we were supposed to go to Borovo Selo. Mr. Stane Brovet was there, he was an officer. I remember that occasion much better because people had been vetted beforehand. I couldn't go, but I found out that everything went well and then I covered the event for the newspapers. And as for this particular occasion, when Mr. Boljkovac came, I talked only to him at the very end of all the meetings that had taken place. I'd rather have him say what was concluded. I didn't want to do that just based on the papers that were provided to us. And then Mr. Boljkovac accepted that after everybody left, he would say something into the microphone and I recorded the conversation. Actually, it was my colleague Jusuf Cehajic, he recorded that interview. He died in shelling. Mr. Boljkovac in haste misplaced that document, everybody was looking for it, and then I asked if he would allow me to look for it. And he allowed me to go through his pockets, through the pockets of his jacket, and I did find the document. I did not have the time to read the document but rather we recorded his words. He gave us a short summary of what was in the document and what had happened during the meeting. And, that I remained in -- on good terms with Mr. Boljkovac and I even had his telephone number in Zagreb, a number that I could call if I needed to ask him something, to inquire about something. He gave me his telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, based on everything you've told us just now about your presence after these talks, I would like to confirm that what's written here, which I believe is in the Vukovarske Novine newspaper, is as you recall. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one might say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, ma'am, in particular, I would just ask you: In this article it's talking about options for easing tensions and takes steps to present individuals from causing unrest. This is also consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, I would tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I note there is a notation in the English saying: "Page 2 missing." I'm not saying that that makes the first page inadmissible but I wish to note that for the record particularly in respect of the witness's second-last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3264, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, we've heard that you worked until the 24th of August, 1991. And now I'd like to ask you to confirm whether certain people whose names I'm going to read out were your colleagues in this time-period between about the 4th of May, 1991, and the 24th of August, 1991. So if I provide their names, I'd like for you to say yes or no if you recall that they were your colleagues at what was then Croatian Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: And if I say yes or no, will you allow me to say something about those people and what I knew about them at the time? I can explain why I'm asking that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, our time is limited today so I do ask you to confine your answer to yes or no --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: -- if you recall them now.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: The first person is Zdravko Seremet. Do you recall that he was a member of Croatian Radio Vukovar during this time period?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Seremet was his name, Seremet, S-e-r-e-m-e-t

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, I have mispronounced his name. Zdravko Seremet, do you recall that he was a member --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And the second --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was nominated and appointed by Minister Hitrec after the correction of the wrong name from the telegram that had arrived before the decision on his appointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And now the second person, I will probably also mispronounce his name but do you recall that Josip Esterajher was one of your colleagues at Croatian Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Josip Esterajher, E-s-t-e-r-a-j-h-e-r, that's how it was spelled at the time. Later on it was Germanised, but at that time that is how it was spelled. Shall I add something? He was appointed as the editor-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And -- excuse me. If you could just -- I think you were getting there, I apologise, that he was an employee of Croatian Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I apologise to the court reporter. My question was for the witness to tell me whether or not he was a member of Croatian Radio Vukovar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on to another person. Do you recall that Sinisa Glavasevic was a member of Croatian Radio Vukovar or, I should say, an employee?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a technician I worked with.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And Branko Polovina, do you recall that he was --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to wait for the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the two of them worked together as a team. Both of them worked with me. At first that's how it was, and then Sinisa took over the management of the radio. After I left he was still there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, I have been asked by the interpreters to suggest that you could please until after I've finished my question. The problem is with the interpretation. The next person I wanted to ask you about is Vesna Vukovic. Do you recall that she was an employee as well?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And Alenka Mirkovic?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Alemka, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And a gentleman named Stjepan Penic. Do you recall that he was also an employee?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he was killed before all the others had joined. All the previous names were the names of the people who joined later in July or August.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And the last person I wanted to ask you about is Svjetlana Polovina, do you recall that she was an employee?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, she was. She was an anchor of a show and she married Branko.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I be allowed to add something? Something about the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, I would like to continue with my questions due to time constraints.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Aha, you have more questions? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, what you've just told us about Mr. Penic, you said that he was killed before all the others had joined. And what I want to ask you is if you know that he was killed -- that there was a member of the Dalj Territorial Defence who bragged that he had killed Stjepan Penic?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Penic lived in Dalj, and the last time he came to the radio was to see me. After that, we heard that he was killed together with a group of people. Stjepan, whom we called Stevo, he was killed, set on fire, and it was my task to organise a commemorative service in Vukovar for him. And just a day before, I was with Sinisa Glavasevic and Branko Polovina, we travelled via Djakovo to the commemorative service in Osijek which was organised by Glas Slavonije.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Just a moment ago you mentioned Sinisa Glavasevic. Do you know what happened to Sinisa Glavasevic after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know then. I heard later, much, much later, recently. I didn't know for a long, long time. I didn't know about anybody, any of my other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could ask for the Registrar's assistance to please pull up 65 ter 6660, which is at tab 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, are you able to see the photograph that's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sinisa.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What is this person's last name, please?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Glavasevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, the caption says that he is in an improvised studio in besieged Vukovar. Did you work from this improvised studio as well?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was still in the official studio until the 24th of August. I don't know what happened after that or where the locations were.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, a moment ago you said that for a long time you didn't know what happened to your colleagues. Do you know now what happened to Sinisa Glavasevic and Branko Polovina?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know when or why or how. I have no information about that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you know that they were killed at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that. I can't tell you when exactly, but this is more recent information. When all sorts of commemorative events were organised and when his young son Bojan was already a grown-up man.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to the time-period that Mirko Stankovic was the editor-in-chief of Radio Vukovar. This is in paragraph 1 of your statement. Now, do you know, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, that after he left Radio Vukovar that he went to go work for Politika, which is Belgrade-based media, I believe?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he worked, but I do know that he continued working in the media as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could have the Registrar's assistance to bring up 65 ter 6659. Your Honour, this is a newspaper article, and due to the size of the print I have made a copy for the witness. If I could please have the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you've indicated that you know that Mirko Stankovic continued to work as a journalist. This is an article that I believe was published in September of 1992 in Vukovarske Novine. I want to ask you, this article says -- the title is: "Commander in a trilby," and there's a photograph of a man identified as Stanko Vujanovic. Do you know who Stanko Vujanovic is?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've not seen this text before. I did not know that there was a newspaper Vukovarske Novine. I thought that everything was over after the fall of Vukovar. I really didn't know that the paper continued being published, and if it did, not a single copy ever reached me. And to be honest, I really didn't care after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you recognise the name of the author? I believe if you turn to -- or if you look on the right page, above the photograph that's been crossed out, can you indicate for us who the author is?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the article was signed by Mirko Stankovic. M, in this case, stands for Mirko. That's his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And I understand that you've not seen this article before. Do you know who Stanko Vujanovic is?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a taxi driver in Vukovar before the war. But I really didn't know anything about him, and there was no reason for him to be of any importance for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: In the time since you returned to Vukovar, during the war period and after, did you ever hear that Stanko Vujanovic was the deputy TO commander, that he was part of the Petrova Gora Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And did you ever hear that he was convicted in 2005 and sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment for the killings at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard stories. When texts were published about former citizens, there were comments about people that people knew. I myself didn't know anybody, nor did I have any contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with Mirko Stankovic in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When we were in Sid, I had his address. His other address. Because the first address was at the house of the mother of director of Radio Sid. Mirko Stankovic caused a fire there. He was thrown out and he was provided with another accommodation. He was very good. He was excellent at propaganda. I believe - I'm not claiming - that a lot of the things that he wrote about had nothing whatsoever to do with the reality of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, if could I ask you to look at the first column on the left side you've been provided, I believe it's the bottom paragraph in the Cyrillic. And the language I want to direct your attention to starts with: "This story followed that path ..."

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where do I start reading?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: The paragraph begins with: "This story followed that path and we will try to help you discover something ..." On the left-hand side, the far bottom column.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what it says here is: "We -- we will try to help you discover something you did not know about another one of our heros from these parts, Stanko Vujanovic." And then the second part that I want to direct your attention to, in your version this would be on the right-hand page. If you could look on the right-hand side, the middle column.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it here? This is where I --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- find it, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, I simply wanted to direct your attention to what Stankovic -- what Mirko Stankovic has said to introduce Mr. Vujanovic. And now if you could -- I realise it's a lengthy article, if you could look at the second page, please. So the right-hand page you have and then in the middle column, the first full paragraph in the middle. And here we have a quote from Stanko Vujanovic. It says: "These two peoples can no longer be together. Any future contact between them would mean a new war, annihilation" --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can somebody come and help me to find this? I simply can't locate the passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'd like to help you. Could we look at the right-hand page? So you see how it is taped together? Yes. And then on the right-hand page, so if you're looking at it in front of you -- yes, the page that's on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would have no objection if the Prosecutor wishes to highlight the passages concerned, if that will assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I would be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. Yes, that would really help me. Let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If the usher could assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let somebody mark the passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Excuse me. If the usher could assist.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are also not seeing the correct page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I feel free to read it, please, just to see what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes. So Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, my question was, I wanted to direct you to this passage where Stanko Vujanovic is quoted. And to make the record clear, this is the section where he says that: "These two peoples can no longer be together," and he mentions that if the Ustashas step on Serbian land, it will be fatal for them and that further contact means a new war. Did you see that section?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, would you agree that it's fair to say that this reporter, Mr. Stankovic, and the publication, which is Vukovarske Novine, are putting Stanko Vujanovic forward as a hero, an important person in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I have no information that he would be so important, and knowing that Mirko Stankovic waged a propaganda war, I don't find it strange that something as ugly as possible, as bad as possible, and almost unreal was written.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would tender this document for admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, P3266.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, earlier today you talked to my learned friend about poetry and about the poetry that was read on Radio Vukovar. First I want to ask you, from your statement, I see that you hosted a programme called "Sundays at Ten." Is this the only programme that you appeared on, on Radio Vukovar? I'm talking about the time-period from 1985 to 1990.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was my permanent obligation, but I also made reports for other shows for the news every day, for the news programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, I have a few questions about one of the exhibits that was admitted with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: This is 1D00456, please, which is Defence tab 1. Excuse me, 2. And Prosecution tab 8. Your Honour, I would like to ask for the usher's assistance to provide a hard copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm interested in the part at the very bottom of the page, the bottom section. And what we have here is a programme from Radio Vukovar and it's for the time-period --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: -- from October 1990 to March 1991. Now, if we look at this programme for Sunday, it has a listing of what's been broadcast between 8.00 a.m. and 11.00 a.m.; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I believe that it's laid out Sunday, Monday, Tuesday --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's there, yes. Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And then if we look at every other day of the week, so Monday through Saturday, it appears that the programming that's listed is from 1.30 p.m. to 5.00 p.m.; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: My question for you is: What was played on the radio at other times? The schedule shows what was played for three to five hours a day, but what was played at other times? What was broadcast?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Lots of music. In my time, various genres, least of all the classical music. Mostly pop, folk. We were obliged to make a list because there was the author's agency, so we had to have a complete list in order to pay what was due.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you did have poetry that was read on your programme. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not just that. It depended. You mean on "Sunday at Ten"?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Or any other programme that you hosted?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the news as well. In the news as short reports after some events. If something happened on the previous day, then on the following day you would say such and such a thing took place. And if it was really worth it, then there would be a shortened version where something short would be reported. Once there was a famous harp player, Rajka Dobronic, and I had to fight to have a report on her in the news as the central information report. I wanted to have an audio recording from her concert. So everything was to be informative and really brief. Even if it was poetry you would say, for example: Yesterday evening in such and such a place a book was published. There we had the audience. The best place was this. We are glad that as the author you agreed to appear, so can you just briefly read to us what you -- and then you say thank you. And it would be all over.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
