utterances.text: So, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, if I understand from your last answer, poetry was read on your programme but also there were other things on your programme, such as the news?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The news were compulsory, but the news were like that because this was a local institution. To inform the public you had to mention all the more important decisions of various organs in the town, and there was not much time left to fit in much of anything else, least of all something that is sheer fun.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what you've described about having topics other than just the local news, in respect of poetry, in particular, how frequently was poetry on the radio?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: But little. Not much. There was no interest. Everyone waited much more for the sports programmes. That was the integral part of every news, every programme, and on the news programme that would be a shortened version. And if there was anything else, then I wouldn't really know because something may have been mentioned in the programmes on languages of various ethnicities. These were hosted by my colleagues who were of that particular ethnicity and I couldn't speak those languages. And as I was not the editor-in-chief, then they were not obliged to provide me with translations or anything like that. We had the Ruthenian and Ukrainian languages. That was the permanent editorial office. We also had Hungarian. That was only the news programme for the day. A lady was doing that part time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We also had Slovakian.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I understand from what you said that there were programmes in other languages. What you've told us is that with your programme, it had mixed content. My question now is: For other journalists who had programmes on Radio Vukovar, did any of them have a programme that was dedicated to poetry?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No one did anything special. We all prepared the daily news programmes together. And then the journalists were in charge of various areas. One was tasked to cover the sports, like I had "Sundays at Ten," and mine was the most mixed. It was the greatest potpourri, that's where anything that may be interesting for the listeners to hear about during one hour would be included. So we would have one report and then one song.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, did you ever hear that other presenters or hosts or journalists would have poetry on their show, possibly in the manner you've indicated where there would be a report and then a song or a report and then some other type of presentation?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No one else did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: But you agree that the other journalists, hosts of radio programmes, that their shows were of a mixed nature as well, that they had, for example, music and news and interviews on their programmes too?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not receiving interpretation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, did you hear my question? If not, we can ask the usher to assist.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't have programmes that would be their personal ones, where they were the authors of the programme like the one on "Sundays at Ten" was. They just made reports for other programmes, for the news programmes and so on, or if it was a children's programme. So they were only in charge of making specific pieces, short presentations or reports. They did not have a term and so that they could say: Well, this is now my time that would be devoted to poetry only or to something else, like I had this specific time that was scheduled for me and then I was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, other persons who worked at the radio also had programmes that they hosted though; right?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And you've said that you -- I asked you if you had heard that other presenters or hosts would have poetry on their programme from time to time. You said you had not heard that. But my question for you now is: If poetry was played on the radio, it would have been played in and amongst other types of material that were broadcast; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's, Mr. President, calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if I could just say one more thing. There have already been two questions asked on this direction. Apparently the Prosecution doesn't like the answers it's getting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I simply wish to be clear on the answer from the witness. I can try to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, that the programmes that were played on Radio Vukovar had mixed content; that is, you would yourself be able to say that you hosted a programme that had different components?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's asked and answered at line 13 and then the answer at line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And if I could ask the witness if she is aware that it was the same for other persons who worked at Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Again that's the same question that was -- that's at line 13 and line 19. That was what that question was about, other people, not the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand that my learned friend's objection has to do with calling for speculation. As Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic who worked there since 1972 and is well versed in the operations of Radio Vukovar, it's simply whether she considers that the other programming was also of a mixed nature. To the best of her knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The objection at this time, Mr. President, is asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please move on, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you indicated that in addition to the programming which we see on the schedule that I provided to you, Radio Vukovar was always on the air and that music was being played; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Were there also advertisements that were played?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And so broadcasting on Radio Vukovar, we see from the schedule that depending on the day, there were seven to 12 programmes, then supplemented by music and advertisements.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And you've stated that you're aware that when somebody published something or they won an award, that their poetry might be read on the radio. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that this is the only time that poetry or other literary publications would be read on the radio?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would say yes. Perhaps only it may be a problem for you or - how should I put it? - it should be simplified, this notion of the programme. The editor-in-chief decided on the programme. That was the standard procedure and it was the standard programme. There were objections that it was boring because people knew exactly when they would hear certain things. And in order to make things less monotonous, then there was the intention, at least in my show on "Sundays at Ten," to make things more colourful. And in other shows, they would be devoted only to specific fields and they could only expand reports connected to the specific subjects. We didn't have anything that was devoted only to poetry or, for example, to music, where somebody would play during an entire time slot. That was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, when you were not at work, when you were not at the office, did you listen to the radio all day, every day?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The editor-in-chief had to do that and the directors were doing that. Later on, it turned out that some people were suspended because they did not provide correct information. He was very strict about it. And no one would ever even think of changing this programme scheme without consulting the editor-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, it was the editor-in-chief who was authorised to determine the programming and it was also the editor-in-chief who was responsible for listening to the radio at all times?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had to because he needed to know what was broadcast, and that was something he was in charge of. Because, otherwise, it wouldn't be serious business if he hadn't known what he was doing. His title was editor-in-chief. I was responsible for my show. The editor of the news programme was held responsible for his news. And we tried to respect truthful and objective reporting, and we tried to provide accurate information.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, in the time-period from 1985 to 1990, you were never the director or editor-in-chief of Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. No. I was first junior journalist and then a journalist and then a junior associate and then editor. You needed years to acquire status. Years of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned before that you thought it was a good thing to try to promote what people were doing in terms of their interests or their hobbies and that on your programme on the radio this is something you tried to broadcast. I'd like to know whether all of the poets that you recall, if they were all equally well known in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not a big town. You have to have in mind how big Vukovar is. So it happened that at some literary events, you would always see the one and the same people. If it was art events, always one and the same people. If it was musical, the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you for a moment --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I could interrupt you for a moment. In particular, you've mentioned Zoran Calic --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Calic. Zoran Calic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And my learned friend asked you about Branko Kovacevic, also a poet. Isn't it true that some of these poets were further along in their poetic interests or careers than others?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Branko was only beginning as a younger man. Zoran Calic definitely even younger. When I mentioned Calic, that was for about three to four years back, but from the time when I presented him to the public for the first time, it's been almost 20 years. That was the period in which he managed to collect all the awards and acknowledgments. But initially, these were the local kids who summoned up courage to do something and then we wanted to encourage them, to present them to the public, and to learn about them, to see what they were doing. There was another one. I don't remember his name any longer but his nickname was Seki. And his first stepping-stone to move forward, so he found support and donors, and then the issue was who wrote about him first. He didn't have many supervisors to speak so, and I even felt unnecessary, in a way, when he said that I had written the first review of whatever he was writing at that time. And I have to say that up until recently, they all very happily remembered those first days of their careers and the occasions on which someone mentioned them publicly for the first time. But perhaps there were those who had no courage to begin working like that and may have gone somewhere further afield. We also had co-operation with Radio Osijek, and we daily sent them reports about major events. It was the Voice of Slavonia and Radio Osijek. The late Stjepan Penic was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I think we have enough from your last answer. If I could ask you my next question, please. I'd like to know if you know of a poet from Vukovar named Ivan Baranjek?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Baranjek?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ivan --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Or perhaps you wanted to ask me about Baranjek.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, Baranjek, Ivan Baranjek.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's difficult, pronunciation of our language. Yes, I knew him. He was on good terms with my father and he used to attend cultural events, but to be honest, I don't remember in what form he published his works, nor have I ever read them. Because from the moment when I began working in the information system, I followed various fields when I was tasked to do so, and then I concentrated on that and did not pay much attention to other fields, nor was I obliged to do that. I even didn't have the right to.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, I understand that you are then familiar with Ivan Baranjek and you said that he was present at cultural events. Did you also know that Ivan Baranjek supported the efforts of persons who were interested in poetry?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ivan Baranjek had published three books of poetry at this time. You said that you weren't familiar with them. I'd like to ask if you knew that he had a studio behind his house where he would have his friends, his acquaintances, other poetry enthusiasts, or his customers around to talk about poetry or paintings?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. For me, it's something completely unknown. First of all, I had no idea where he lived or what he had there, in terms of equipment, and if he had something like that, then I think it was -- he kept a low profile. It was not made public. Or at least I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you do know, though, that Ivan Baranjek was somebody who wrote poetry. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But what kind and such-like, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And did you know that his poetry was read on Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not while I had the obligation to do that type of work. Perhaps before I came to the radio or while I was in charge of other departments, and I cannot comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that he did not read his poetry or his poetry was not read on your show?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And when did you first hear of a poet from Pacetin named Branko Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the year. I just know that he's younger than me and that he -- how should I put it? He was a bit insistent. He offered himself and he sent invitations, and I knew him as the younger brother of my classmate. She used to be my best friend in one period, and so I looked at it and it was very nicely organised. The whole town was informed and then they came to the museum hall. It was all prepared as if a very distinguished guest would be there. And, therefore, I covered the event in an appropriate manner. In such places, we would have celebrations promoting books, for example, of Djordje Radosevic, who was a native of Vukovar, and he was a writer now residing in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He had received all possible state and international --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to cut you off. I think we've strayed past what my question was, and I note that it is the time for the second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Clanton. Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, we take the second break, 30 minutes. We'll be back at 12.45. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, I'd like to briefly go back to something that we discussed before the break. We were talking about the Vukovar poet whose name was Ivan Baranjek and I asked you if you knew that his poetry was read on Radio Vukovar. This is at page 55 of the temporary transcript. And what you said was that it was not, and I'm going to quote, "not while I had the obligation to do that type of work." Is there a time that you were not in a position to know or you were not obligated to do the type of work that would relate to a poet like Ivan Baranjek having his work read on the radio?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That could only be while I was on maternity leave for a year, after the birth of my son. That was in 1975 and one part of 1976.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you continue in your answer, you said: "Perhaps before I came to the radio or while I was in charge of other departments ..." Can you confirm there was a time you were in charge of other departments?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want me to go through the whole chronology of my employment?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could that be of any interest --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you was that you've indicated that there was a time when you were in charge of other departments and that you wouldn't be able to say for sure --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be instructed not to interrupt the Prosecutor during the question, to wait for the question to end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Madam Brlic-Jovanovic, please don't interrupt the Prosecutor while she is still putting the question to you. Just wait until she has finished. If not, we have a problem of overlapping and that's a problem for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, to go back to my question, without going through the chronology of your employment, just to confirm that you've said there was a time you were in charge of other departments and it's therefore possible that Ivan Baranjek's poetry was read at that time?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, we were talking about Branko Kovacevic before the break. I asked you about when you first became aware of him, and you said you did not recall the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could have the Registrar's assistance, please, to provide 1D00484. And that's at tab 9. And I do have a paper copy for the witness, if the usher would assist, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you did not recall the year when you first became aware of the poet Branko Kovacevic. The document I'm showing has been provided, I believe, from one of his publications and it lists his involvement in various poetry collections. And if we look at this document, it says: "He has co-authored the following collections of poetry." And then it listed five -- four, excuse me, collections that were all published between 1981 and 1983. The first one is called "Hazy Gaze" and the last one is "Arches of the Future." And I want to ask if seeing this limited biography of Mr. Kovacevic which contains some of his publications helps refresh your memory about the time that you first became aware of a published poet named Branko Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first book of his does ring a distant bell, and I mean his first independent book of poetry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: This is the one listed as "Enthusiasm of the Sprout"?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I do recall that title. It sticks in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Madam Witness, we don't have a date of that publication, "Enthusiasm of the Sprout," but what I want to ask you is if these other publications, which were published in the early 1980s, help refresh your memory on whether Mr. Kovacevic was a poet who was known to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The titles don't tell me much. The only one that seems to still be present in my memory is the last one, "The Enthusiasm of the Sprout." I seem to be able to associate that title with that name. The rest, no. Doesn't tell me much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, did you know that Goran Hadzic and Branko Kovacevic were friends?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, in your statement, you've talked about and we've already discussed some of your professional obligations, your responsibilities, and one of those responsibilities was to monitor the Vukovar Municipal Assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And it said in your statement that the first time you met Goran Hadzic was when he was an SDS, Serbian Democratic Party, assemblyman at the Vukovar Municipal Assembly. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just a remark, if I may. I didn't actually meet him, but I noticed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, this is -- the time-period I'm talking about is before the incident in Borovo Selo in May of 1991. And you told us today, which is at page 7 of the transcript, that you interviewed Goran Hadzic and other prominent leaders of some political parties after the events in Plitvice. Do you recall the names of the other people --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall the names of the other persons who were on the programme with Goran Hadzic at that time?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic. Mercep. I can't be positive about any of the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And was Goran Hadzic, if you recall, introduced as a member of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Was he introduced as a member of the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And at the time that you interviewed Mr. Hadzic, Mr. Dokmanovic, and Mr. Mercep, was Goran Hadzic well known as somebody who had been arrested at Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And so, Madam Witness, your knowledge of Mr. Hadzic at the time was as a politician, the time being 1991, and not as a poet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't look like one, did he?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: In your statement, you've said at paragraph 4 that you don't know if Goran Hadzic privately wrote poems. Do you recall saying that to the investigator for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And earlier this morning, I asked you if it was correct that you did not have any personal or social relationship with Goran Hadzic, either in the 1990s or now, and you said that you did not. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, no. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I should break my question into two parts. I apologise for the confusion. This morning I asked you --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you should, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Okay. This morning I asked you whether you had a personal or social relationship with Goran Hadzic. Do you remember that I asked you that question?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And when I asked you that question this morning, you said that did you not have a personal or social relationship with Goran Hadzic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And so, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, is it fair to say that you didn't know at the time, in 1991, about any of Mr. Hadzic's personal interests?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact, no, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: So, for example, you didn't know that he was interested in karate?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And you didn't know that he was interested in training dogs either?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Were you aware that Goran Hadzic attended Branko Kovacevic's poetry reading?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And did you also, then, not know that he did so after being invited by Branko Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat your last question. But only your last question, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Did you know that Goran Hadzic attended the poetry reading of Branko Kovacevic after being invited by Branko Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: But this is not something you knew at the time for a fact?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, did you know that Goran Hadzic read poetry with his girlfriend?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: The next thing I want to ask you about has to do with the role of the radio during the time that Vukovar was under siege. During the time that you worked for Croatian Radio Vukovar, would you agree with me that the radio was an important method for sharing of information?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And would you agree that during the summer of 1991, that it was known that there was Croatian Radio Vukovar that was operating in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that this was known in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was our duty to send daily reports to Zagreb about our operations and our shows and any other information of significance for the entire state. It was our obligation to broadcast that from Vukovar studio, and that was announced as being broadcast from Vukovar for the entire territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: So, based on your last answer, is it fair to say that this would also have been known in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. That's calling for speculation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you confirmed that you knew that the broadcasts and the fact that there were broadcasts was known in Zagreb. Do you know if this was the same in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to know who was listening to what and where. But it would have only been expected because communications were free-flowing. There was freedom of communication. So anybody could follow anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And is it correct that a person with a radio in the Vukovar area could pick up the signal of a broadcast from another area that was not too far away?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We always monitored the Radio Vukovar range because before the 1990s, the technology was -- was renewed. But there were areas where one could follow our broadcast as well as areas where one couldn't. However, this is a technical issue which I cannot comment upon. I can't tell you exactly how far our broadcasts reached and where we could be heard without any technical problems and where not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could please have 65 ter 6662, which is at tab 32.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, this document is only in English so I'm going to read what it says and it will be translated to you.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: This document is a report from Radio Belgrade and it's entitled: "Radio on Croatian synchronised attacks." Now the attack is the 26th of August, 1991. I understand that you had stopped working two days before the 26th of August. Now, what I want to ask you about, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, in this text we see that Radio Belgrade is reporting on what they were told by Ilija Kojic, who was the minister of the Territorial Defence in the government of the SBWS, Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. The radio was reporting about attacks on particular villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And for Your Honours, if we look at the third paragraph down, I'd like to read what this Radio Belgrade report says. It says: "Information and programmes broadcast by the Croatian Radio Vukovar are not only incorrect, but are also directly adding fuel to the fire. For instance, the radio broadcast the invention that nine tanks of the Yugoslav People's Army have been destroyed so far. The fact is that so far only one tank has been hit and that it has already been repaired. Vukovar Radio is also appealing to women to form a human barrier and stop the units of the Yugoslav People's Army." That's the end of the quote.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, my question for you, what I want to ask is that based on what I have read to you from a Radio Belgrade report, does that help you affirm whether or not the reports of Croatian Radio Vukovar were themselves part of the news?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness does not have this document in her own language. I think it would at the least to be fair to tell her the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I indicated the date. It was the 26th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you need me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. After the 24th of August, which was the last day I went to work, I had no information as to who broadcast what. However, I knew something else. While I was still there, before I suffered a serious leg injury, some misinformation was broadcast with a view to spreading propaganda. I can corroborate that by saying that the chief of the police administration in Vukovar, Mr. Stipo Pole even requested that nobody be sent for written daily reports on the situation on the ground because he wanted only me to come to fetch those reports. Otherwise he thought that -- that there would only be confusion on the ground and he would suffer unpleasant consequences. That is why he left his telephone number in his drawer. He said jokingly that if I was interested in anything else, that I should call him, because he didn't trust anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I told him if I couldn't come myself that --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I apologise. I have limited time so I'm going to move on from --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can see it at the end. At the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, I understand that you stopped working on the 24th of August and what you've said is that you had no information after that date about who broadcast what. I've read you this excerpt from Radio Belgrade as an example to ask you whether you would agree that during the time-period, let's say, the month of August, 1991, when you were at radio -- Croatian Radio Vukovar, that you knew that your news was itself part of the news that was being broadcast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, first, I think the question is vague. And, secondly, because the document itself sources a person as being the basis for the information, it -- it's not actually clear that the proposition or that the basis for the question exists. That there's a source cited. So it's actually not clear that the broadcast is being heard elsewhere -- if that's what my friend means, and I'm not sure from the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it would perhaps clarify, the report is from a person named Branko Pjetlovic. My understanding is that this is the person who read the report or was responsible for its dissemination on Radio Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Gosnell. I'm trying to understand. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But it's the first five lines that indicate where the information came from, and we don't know where that person mentioned, i.e., Mr. Kojic, was at the time that he conveyed that information to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did indicate when I first pulled up this document that there was a quotation attributed to Mr. Kojic and that it was about the attack, the co-ordinated attack in these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, that's not the problem. The problem is that there's a question about, isn't it true that -- that this radio station was the basis or was being heard elsewhere. And that's the part that, I think, is assumed. It hasn't been established.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: That is the question for the witness, Mr. President. If this document assists her in considering whether she knew at the time, and I said August 1991, that the broadcasts of Croatian Radio Vukovar were being reported on, monitored elsewhere; for example, Radio Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Didn't she answer that one?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise, I do not think that she has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think she did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what I was -- that is what I intended to suggest, Ms. Clanton. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, are you aware that in June of 1991, Serb or Serbian Radio for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was established?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, did you ever hear that Mirko Stankovic was the head of Serbian or Serb Radio, that was set up in late June 1991?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. But I would ask you for permission to add a question; namely, where was the seat or the headquarters of that newly formed radio station?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I can show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could please have 1D00605, which is at tab 36. And for this one, I would need to provide a hard copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, I've put a square brackets around the paragraph. Are you able to see it?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see it, but it's blurred and it's impossible to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, I have a --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: It would be page 2 in the English, please. And it's the very last paragraph of the article which I've provided to the witness. As she has difficulty reading it, may I have Your Honours permission to read the short paragraph to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, this report says the following in quotes: "A Serbian Radio report from Borovo Selo managed to reach Vukovar using an indirect route. The weak station is sending its information via other, more powerful radio stations. According to this information, life in Borovo Selo was normal today. In other words, it was only exposed to sniper fire, while the heavy weapons were silent. Borovo Selo made a hasty assessment of the damage that was caused by three days of continuous attacks from Borovo Naselje. According to the Serbian Radio, many houses were damaged, especially on the southern side of the village." Now, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you asked me about the area or the place where Serbian Radio for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was located. This article suggests that they were reporting from Borovo Selo, and I want to know if this refreshes your memory about the establishment of Serbian Radio for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I'm not familiar with this detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am aware that I'm running out of time. I have one more question on this subject and then I had one other brief question for the witness. With Your Honours' leave, could I please continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you recall that when I asked you questions this morning, I asked you about your colleagues, including Vesna Vukovic and Sinisa Glavasevic. You indicated that they were working at Croatian Radio Vukovar in the summer of 1991. Do you remember that testimony? I'm sorry, ma'am, the answer was not recorded on the transcript. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is waiting for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were added as assistants to the office of the Croatian Radio Vukovar. They just arrived one day and said: We'll be working with you from today on. And there were also two girls in addition to them. Now what their names were, I can't really remember. They were also at the disposal if the permanently employed journalists from the editorial office needed any help. But there was no competition or anything. I don't know how these persons -- except for Sinisa Glavasevic, who was employed by decision of the commission earlier, and Vesna Vukovic and Alemka Mirkovic simply appeared there. It was said that they were the assistants to help the old journalists who were the members of the editorial office from before, and the other two girls I mentioned who weren't there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I think you've answered my question. Is it correct that oftentimes Sinisa Glavasevic and Vesna Vukovic worked as a team?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know at that time while I was still there, the team was Sinisa Glavasevic and Branko Polovina as the logistics, if I may put it so. And how this was divided later, who would be doing what and who would be helping whom, that's something that I couldn't know. The only thing I know for sure is that Sinisa Glavasevic and Branko Polovina would go to Zagreb, even during the first air-strikes, and they took the recordings --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic, I'm going to stop you there. I believe you have answered my question. I would like to show you a passage of a book. The narrator here is Vesna Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And if I could ask for the Registrar to please bring up 65 ter 6658, which is at tab 28. And I have a paper copy for the witness, if the usher could assist. If we could have the second page, please. And also the next page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, the passage that I circled, since you have a copy, I'm not going to read it. Have you had a chance to read it?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: For Your Honours, this is the paragraph that starts with: "However, in early August ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now in this paragraph we see that Vesna Vukovic is recounting a conversation she had with Sinisa Glavasevic and they saw something that they said was Stankovic's contribution to Novi Sad TV. Ma'am, would you agree with me that they're talking about Mirko Stankovic here? Perhaps it would be of assistance as well if we look at the paragraph above the one that I circled. It says: "We did not see Mirko Stankovic," and it says that he was in Borovo Selo and Negoslavci. So am I -- if you could just listen to my question.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Is it correct that they're referring to Mirko Stankovic in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what they're talking about is a report from Mirko Stankovic that was on Novi Sad TV. My question is: While you were working at Croatian Radio Vukovar, did you ever hear about what was broadcast on Novi Sad TV?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: We see here that your colleagues were able to see what was broadcast on Novi Sad TV. Did you ever watch Novi Sad TV?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. May I say something? All this, what Mirko Stankovic could publish, was part of the propaganda war which I mentioned to you at the beginning. And this second part, this conversation, is something based on memory, and it is a part of something written by a third person. It's something re-told. And when someone wants to achieve something while re-telling, then he can make all sorts of things out of it. So I do not believe the first, the second, or the third element here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you just said that this was part of the propaganda war which you had mentioned to us before, and my question is: Were reports by Mr. Stankovic or others that you would consider to be propaganda, were they known to you when you were still working in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you've said that this was something that was being done for propaganda purposes. Are you saying that the propaganda wasn't something that you heard?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, you've discussed your programme on Radio Vukovar and briefly your career as a journalist. Why didn't you work as a journalist after you returned to Vukovar in 1991?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I first had to resolve where I would live. Then I had to take care of my ill husband, his elderly mother, because everyone else, my whole family, the relatives on his side because there were no longer any left of mine, we were looking for a place to live. Then we looked for a way to provide treatment to my late husband. And then it was my personal decision to never work in journalism. Because simply I was disgusted with everything, on all sides. I prefer that everything be known and then let us see but not have someone try to brainwash you with some other information. My decision was not to work as a journalist any longer. And after the peaceful reintegration it was offered to me start working again in the same line of work, but I said thank you and I decided that I didn't want to. My husband was in a critical condition. He had had strokes and gangrene and he was in a wheelchair and so on and so forth, and I could not accept any daily obligations any longer to be away from home, and no one coerced me to that in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you described during your testimony this morning that you were at Velepromet from approximately the 12th to the 14th of November, 1991. And I wanted to ask you what -- what kind of -- what kind of armed forces or military groups did you see while you were at Velepromet on those dates?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: All who were walking around there wore uniforms. I could recognise some people from the earlier peacetime life. Those were representatives of the civilian police from Vukovar. There were also people wearing military uniforms whom I did not know. I recognised the commander - how would we call him? - the director of Velepromet, Milovan Cvetkovic. I'm sorry, I stand corrected, Milovan Cvjeticanin, with a J.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, did you see persons who were dressed as Chetnik or -- Chetnik volunteers?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And did you recognise anybody who appeared to be part of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how I would have been able to distinguish between the Territorial Defence and the regular army. I didn't know the insignia or who wore whose uniforms, who got which uniforms, because sometimes even elderly ladies would be taken out of basements and they had nothing to wear so they would put on some thick, coarse woollen coats and trousers which may have seemed ridiculous but they didn't have anything. I received footwear for the first time because in the basement I was wearing pink summer slippers and I had some sort of skiing winter jacket, and then they found footwear for me that I could walk in.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, you described the room you were in at Velepromet and that you received rice and there were pallets to sleep on. If you recall, were --

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a room. It was a section of the basement where shells couldn't kill people who were down there. It was some sort of underground warehouse. There were pallets and there were all of us who came from this one basement and other people. We did receive good blankets, thick ones, and there was a very small stove, and that was an area perhaps bigger than this courtroom. And people lay one next to the other like sardines, and curfew was imposed so people couldn't walk around as they wished. The first evening, no provision of food was organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, if I could interrupt you, please. If you recall the room -- I'm sorry, the warehouse area that you were in, were most of the people in that room Serbs or were they Croats?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mixed. From our sector of the fair-ground, as they arrived, they were all mixed. Our former neighbours, even people whose children were wearing the ZNG uniforms and others who not in such a situation. And everyone was sad, in a very dejected mood, desperate that something like that had happened. The last supply of food that we had, we carried it, some meat that we could cut. We carried it with us because we didn't know how long everything would last, so that we wouldn't starve. We had no water left and that was the last food we had. If Radoslav needed it, he was a diabetic and he couldn't live without medication and food. So I brought that and I distributed it among people I knew and those I didn't. It -- it was like Jesus when he had three fish and then he managed to feed a great number of people. So whenever you saw anyone else that was still alive, you would be happy because there were people that you didn't know about. And it was no longer important who was a Serb or a Croat. They were happy that they had managed to leave the underground torture that they had gone through.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Clanton. Mr. Gosnell, anything in re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. President. May we have 1D456, please, which is Defence tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, how many years in total did you work at Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from 1972, 2nd June 1972, until the 24th of August, 1991. There was a period of one year when Igor was about to be born and he was born in 1976, so between mid-1975 and mid-1976. So my years of pensionable employment were calculated as 18 years and -- 18-odd year, less than 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how many years did you work at the programme "On Sundays at Ten"?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The last few years. Because those who had been there before me at the radio worked on that programme. I can't say exactly when that -- but, in any case, from the moment when I got employment, I had to be questioned so they would determine whether I would be capable of doing the work. It was at the same time --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you, Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, and I do apologise. When you say "a few years," was it more or less than three years that you were working on "On Sundays at Ten"?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: More than three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And looking at the schedule, the radio schedule, in the English, I'd like to turn to page 2, please, and look under "Saturday." And everyone can rest assured that I'm not going to go through every single programme but I'd like to go through a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The first item at 1300 hours on Saturday: "Overview of the day's programme." Ever hear any local poets interviewed there or any poetry read during that programme?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What about for the next item: "KALI-EPP of local radio stations (folk music)," ever hear any local poets interviewed or poetry recited on that?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "Music Evergreens (popular music)," ever hear any local poets interviewed on that or any poetry recited?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It couldn't have been so because the speaker who announced that programme was on duty in the afternoon and he played both music and he announced things and he did everything himself. He did not have orders or authorisation to include the sort of reports that you mentioned in the programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "News and market barometer," any poets interviewed or poetry recited?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What about on "Together on Saturdays"?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Preparations for weekends were already under way and proposals relative to weekends, there was a show title: "What to do on the weekend," and there were proposals as to where to go, what to see in Baranja, an outing Valpovo, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the programming on each of these channels -- on each of those programmes?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When we prepared shows we always had discussions at the editorial board, so whenever something happened, I was the one who was reproached for insisting on fine art or excavations in Vucin Dol, the others insisted on sports, and there were also those who didn't want to participate in economic shows because they thought that they were boring. But pretty much things did not depend on us. We would be invited to press conferences and meetings from which we had to report. We had to have commercials and -- because they were paid. We had music shows that had to meet all sorts of requirements and they had to suit all the tastes. They -- we had to play music from all over the world or Yugoslavia, of all genres, pop music, folk music. And we did not exclude anybody, the old settlers or the newcomers. The only thing that we did not play were the so-called ganga music. If somebody decided to play that, I'm sure that the editors would have hanged themselves. This may sound flippant but we never played ganga.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So the content of the radio programmes on this schedule was discussed at these editorial board meetings that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not every day. But meetings did not have to be officially announced. There would always be comments, people discussed things among themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did any of the programmes on this schedule, not just Saturday but the rest of the week, did any of them, to your knowledge, let's say, over the course of the last ten years that you worked there, did any of them have interviews with local poets or poetry recitations other than "On Sunday at Ten"?

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You said during your cross-examination that Goran Hadzic did not look like a poet. Can you tell us what you meant by that, please.

utterances.speaker: KARMEN BRLIC-JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not a psychiatrist or psychologist, so I really can't say anything of much importance. I can just speculate. But I don't think that I'm well suited to provide any comments. I don't want to offend anybody. However, in my view, he should be more talkative. He should be a man of more words, like me, for example. He should be a playful soul; whereas he was a very serious gentleman. I really can't go on commenting. I seem be misbehaving, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, thank you very much. That concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Brlic-Jovanovic, this concludes your testimony. We thank you again for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back home. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If there's not -- nothing else, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not for today, Your Honours. Our next witness will be here tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of September, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.53 p.m.,
